question: What is the long-term capital gains tax rate on listed equity shares under Section 112A for FY 2025-26?
ground_truth: Long-term capital gains on listed equity shares held for more than 12 months are taxed at 12.5% (increased from 10% in Budget 2024) on gains exceeding Rs 1.25 lakh per financial year under Section 112A, provided STT was paid at acquisition. Gains up to Rs 1.25 lakh are exempt.

question: How are short-term capital gains on equity taxed if shares are sold within 12 months?
ground_truth: Short-term capital gains on listed equity shares held for 12 months or less are taxed at 20% under Section 111A (raised from 15% in July 2024), plus applicable cess. STT must have been paid on the sale transaction.

question: What is the basic exemption limit under the new tax regime for FY 2025-26?
ground_truth: Under the new tax regime (Section 115BAC) for FY 2025-26, the basic exemption limit is Rs 3 lakh. A full rebate under Section 87A makes income up to Rs 7 lakh tax-free, and marginal relief applies up to Rs 7.27 lakh.

question: Explain the old vs new tax regime choice and the Form 10-IEA filing requirement for salaried individuals.
ground_truth: Salaried individuals can choose between old and new regimes each financial year. To opt out of the new regime (which is now default), they must file Form 10-IEA before filing ITR. Business income taxpayers can switch only once. The new regime offers lower slabs but forgoes most deductions like 80C and HRA.

question: What are the income tax slabs under the new regime for FY 2025-26?
ground_truth: New regime slabs FY 2025-26: 0-3L nil, 3-6L 5%, 6-9L 10%, 9-12L 15%, 12-15L 20%, above 15L 30%. Surcharge and 4% health and education cess apply on base tax. Rebate under 87A eliminates tax up to 7L.

question: How is indexation benefit treated for debt mutual funds redeemed after April 2023?
ground_truth: For debt mutual funds purchased after 1 April 2023, indexation benefit was withdrawn. Gains are taxed at slab rate as per Finance Act 2023, regardless of holding period. Funds bought before 1 April 2023 and held beyond 36 months still enjoyed 20% with indexation until the 2024 Budget removed indexation for unlisted asset classes prospectively.

question: What is the surcharge rate for income above Rs 2 crore under the new regime?
ground_truth: Under the new regime, surcharge is capped at 25% for total income exceeding Rs 2 crore (reduced from 37% under old regime in 2023). Highest effective rate including 4% cess is about 39% for income above 2 crore.

question: How is TDS on sale of property under Section 194IA calculated and what is the threshold?
ground_truth: TDS under Section 194IA is 1% on sale consideration or stamp duty value, whichever is higher, for property transactions where consideration is Rs 50 lakh or more. Buyer must deposit via Form 26QB and issue Form 16B to seller. No threshold relief for joint purchases aggregated.

question: What is the standard deduction available under the new tax regime for salaried employees in FY 2025-26?
ground_truth: Standard deduction of Rs 50,000 is available under the new regime for salaried individuals and pensioners from FY 2023-24 onwards. An additional Rs 15,000 was proposed for family pensioners. This is automatically applied and replaces earlier transport and medical allowances.

question: Describe the sunset clause for the new manufacturing tax regime under Section 115BAB.
ground_truth: Section 115BAB offers a 15% concessional rate for new domestic manufacturing companies incorporated after 1 October 2019 and commencing production before 31 March 2024. Companies had to opt by filing Form 10-ID. After the sunset date, new entrants cannot avail 15%; they fall under 115BA (22%) or normal rates.

question: How are dividends taxed in the hands of investors after DDT abolition?
ground_truth: From FY 2020-21, DDT was abolished. Dividends are taxable in the investor's hands at slab rate. Companies deduct TDS at 10% if dividend exceeds Rs 5,000 per year per investor. Resident individuals can submit Form 15G/H for nil TDS if income below threshold.

question: What are the capital gains implications when switching between new and old tax regimes mid-year for business income?
ground_truth: Switching regimes does not by itself trigger capital gains. Capital gains are computed per asset holding period and taxed under Sections 112, 112A, and 111A irrespective of slab regime. However, regime choice affects set-off and carry-forward benefits like 80C deductions that can affect net tax payable on same gains.

question: What is the lock-in and tax treatment for ELSS mutual fund investments?
ground_truth: ELSS has a 3-year lock-in, the shortest among 80C instruments. Investment up to Rs 1.5 lakh qualifies for 80C deduction. LTCG on redemption beyond Rs 1.25 lakh is taxed at 12.5% under 112A. Dividends, if opted, are taxed at slab rate.

question: How does Section 54EC allow capital gains exemption and what are its limits?
ground_truth: Section 54EC allows exemption of LTCG from land/building if gains are invested in NHAI/REC bonds within 6 months. Investment capped at Rs 50 lakh per financial year, lock-in 5 years, and interest is taxable. Proportionate exemption applies if only part of gains is invested.

question: What changes to TDS on rent under Section 194I versus 194IB should tenants note?
ground_truth: Section 194I applies to rent paid by businesses: 2% for plant/machinery, 10% for land/building when annual rent exceeds Rs 2.4 lakh. Section 194IB applies to individuals/HUF not under audit paying rent >Rs 50,000 per month, deducting 5% and depositing via Form 26QC without TAN. HRA exemption requires actual rent receipts and landlord PAN if rent > Rs 1 lakh annually.

question: How is indexation benefit calculated for debt mutual fund redemptions after April 2023 for pre-2023 investments?
ground_truth: Debt funds bought before 1 April 2023 retained indexation benefit if held beyond 36 months until Budget 2024 proposed changes for specified mutual funds. Indexed cost = actual cost * (CII year of sale / CII year of purchase). LTCG taxed at 20% after indexing. Post-April 2023 purchases are slab-taxed with no indexation regardless of holding.

question: What is the difference between direct and regular mutual fund plans in terms of expense ratio and NAV?
ground_truth: Direct plans have lower expense ratios (typically 0.5-1% less) because no distributor commission is paid. Consequently, direct plan NAVs are slightly higher and returns compound higher over time. Regular plans include trail commission for advisors. Portfolio and fund manager are identical.

question: How are systematic investment plans (SIPs) taxed when units are redeemed on a first-in-first-out basis?
ground_truth: Each SIP installment is treated as a separate investment. On redemption, FIFO applies: earliest units are deemed sold first. If latest SIP is under 12 months for equity funds, STCG 20% applies to that portion; older installments held >12 months attract LTCG 12.5% beyond Rs 1.25 lakh exemption.

question: What is the total expense ratio (TER) limit for equity mutual funds under SEBI guidelines?
ground_truth: SEBI caps TER for equity funds at 2.25% for first Rs 500 crore AUM, then slab-graded down to 1.05% for very large AUMs. Additional 5 bps for exit-load credit and 30 bps for B-30 city inflows are permitted within limits. ETFs have lower caps around 1% as of 2024 update.

question: How can an investor use systematic transfer plans (STP) to manage lump-sum deployment risk?
ground_truth: STP moves a fixed sum periodically from a liquid or ultra-short fund into an equity fund, averaging entry cost and reducing timing risk. Amounts transferred from debt fund may attract STCG/LTCG depending on holding period of source scheme. STPs can be registered for 6-24 months with daily/weekly/monthly frequency.

question: What is the cut-off time for same-day NAV applicability for equity mutual fund purchases?
ground_truth: For equity funds, purchase requests received before 3:00 PM with funds realized get same-day NAV. After 3 PM, next business day's NAV applies. Redemption cut-off is also 3 PM. NAVs are declared by 11 PM on AMFI website. Non-business days shift to next trading day.

question: Explain the risk-o-meter changes introduced by SEBI in 2024 and their impact on fund selection.
ground_truth: SEBI mandated 6-tier risk-o-meter (Low to Very High) based on portfolio volatility, updated monthly. Any change in category requires 30-day notice and exit-load waiver. For example, a large-cap fund may show 'Very High' despite equity tag due to concentration, guiding conservative investors to hybrid funds.

question: How do overnight funds differ from liquid funds in portfolio and taxation?
ground_truth: Overnight funds invest only in securities maturing in one day, offering near-zero duration risk, while liquid funds hold up to 91-day papers. Both are debt funds; after April 2023, gains are taxed at slab regardless of holding. Overnight funds have lowest expense and are used for treasury parking with T+1 redemption.

question: What is portfolio rebalancing and how often should a retirement-focused mutual fund portfolio be rebalanced?
ground_truth: Rebalancing restores target allocation (e.g., 60% equity/40% debt) after market drift. For retirement investors, annual or semi-annual rebalancing is recommended, or when deviation exceeds 5%. Automatic trigger-based STPs can rebalance without manual trades, but capital gains tax should be considered for debt shifts.

question: How do flexi-cap funds manage allocation across market caps compared to multi-cap funds?
ground_truth: Flexi-cap funds have no minimum allocation per market cap and can dynamically allocate 0-100% across large/mid/small as per manager view, with at least 65% in equity for tax equity status. Multi-cap funds mandated in 2020 must invest at least 25% each in large, mid, and small caps, reducing manager flexibility but ensuring diversification.

question: What is the procedure to update nominee details for mutual fund folios online after March 2024?
ground_truth: From June 2024, SEBI allowed two-factor authentication e-nomination via MF Central or AMC portal using PAN and OTP. Investors can add up to three nominees with percentage share, or opt out with declaration. Physical nomination requires witness. Nominee change does not require closing folio and overrides earlier will unless will specifically revokes it depending on succession law.

question: How is NAV calculated for mutual funds and why does dividend payout reduce NAV?
ground_truth: NAV = (Market value of securities + receivables - liabilities) / Outstanding units. When a dividend is paid, equivalent amount leaves AUM, so NAV drops by dividend per unit plus statutory levy. IDCW option reflects this; growth option retains profits, so NAV stays higher. Record date determines entitlement.

question: What documents are required for a health insurance claim rejection appeal?
ground_truth: For appeal, submit: original rejection letter, duly filled claim form, hospital bills with break-up, discharge summary, investigation reports, doctor's prescription, ID proof, policy copy, and a cover letter explaining medical necessity. Include TPA email trails. IRDAI mandates insurer response within 15 days of appeal via grievance cell; escalate to Ombudsman if unresolved after 30 days.

question: How does the IRDAI standard definition of pre-existing disease affect waiting periods?
ground_truth: IRDAI defines pre-existing disease as any condition diagnosed or treated within 36 months before policy inception. Standard waiting period is 2-4 years before PED is covered. From April 2024, maximum waiting was capped at 3 years for most policies; insurers must disclose PED loading transparently. Continuous renewal reduces waiting cumulatively.

question: What is the free-look period for life and health insurance policies under current IRDAI rules?
ground_truth: Policyholders have a 30-day free-look period from receipt of policy document to return it if terms are unsatisfactory, receiving premium refund minus proportionate risk and stamp duty. For electronic policies, receipt date is email delivery. Insurer must refund within 7 days.

question: How are health insurance claims settled when treatment is taken at a non-network hospital?
ground_truth: Non-network treatment follows reimbursement: insured pays first, then submits bills within 15 days post-discharge for claim filing within policy period. Insurer reimburses admissible amount per room rent sub-limits and co-pay. Pre-authorization is not needed but intimation within 24 hours of emergency admission is mandatory.

question: What are the common reasons for health insurance claim rejection and how can they be avoided?
ground_truth: Common rejections: non-disclosure of PED, treatment beyond policy limits, consumables exclusion, claim filed after deadline, and hospitalization under 24 hours without day-care cover. Avoid by disclosing full history, checking sub-limits, and intimating insurer within 48 hours. Keep original bills and ensure hospital is registered with 10+ inpatient beds.

question: Describe the IRDAI standard turnaround times for cashless pre-authorization and final claim settlement.
ground_truth: Insurers must approve initial cashless authorization within 3 hours of request. Final claim settlement or repudiation must be intimated within 30 days of receiving last necessary document. If investigation is needed, decision within 45 days. Interest at 2% above bank rate is payable for delays.

question: How does the no-claim bonus (NCB) work in health insurance versus motor insurance?
ground_truth: Health NCB typically increases sum insured by 10-50% per claim-free year without extra premium, cumulative up to 100%. Some products offer premium discount instead. Motor NCB gives premium discount on own-damage (20% year1 up to 50% year5) and is transferable across vehicles but not across insurers without proof; health NCB is non-transferable and resets after claim.

question: What is the role of the Insurance Ombudsman and when can a policyholder approach them?
ground_truth: Ombudsman resolves disputes up to Rs 50 lakh for claim rejection, short settlement, or mis-selling. Policyholder must first lodge written grievance with insurer and wait 30 days or receive repudiation, then file with Ombudsman within one year via Bima Bharosa or in person. Award is binding on insurer if accepted by complainant within 30 days.

question: How do restoration benefits work in comprehensive health insurance plans?
ground_truth: Restoration replenishes sum insured after partial or full exhaustion in a policy year, for unrelated illness only, once per year in most plans. Some newer plans offer unlimited restoration for same illness after 45-day gap. Restored amount cannot be carried forward and is not available for first claim of year; it triggers only after primary sum is used.

question: What is the claim process for term life insurance death benefit and what evidence is mandatory?
ground_truth: Nominee must intimate insurer within 30 days, submitting death certificate, original policy bond, KYC of nominee, and medical cause of death if death within 3 years of policy start. For accidental death, FIR and post-mortem required. Insurer must settle within 30 days of complete submission; early claims (<3 years) may invoke investigation under Section 45 of Insurance Act, extending to 120 days.

question: What is the maximum tax deduction under Section 80CCD(1B) for NPS Tier I contributions?
ground_truth: An additional deduction of Rs 50,000 under 80CCD(1B) is available exclusively for NPS Tier I contributions, over and above Rs 1.5 lakh under 80C+80CCD(1). Thus total deduction for NPS can be up to Rs 2 lakh if 80CCD(2) employer portion (up to 10% basic salary, 14% for government) is also claimed.

question: How does the NPS Tier II account differ from Tier I in terms of withdrawal and tax benefits?
ground_truth: Tier I is locked until 60 with limited premature exits and offers tax benefits under 80CCD. Tier II is voluntary, has no lock-in (except for government employees claiming 80C with 3-year lock), offers no tax deduction except for government staff, and allows anytime withdrawal. Tier I requires min Rs 500 opening and Rs 1,000 yearly; Tier II needs no minimum balance.

question: What are the annuity and lump sum withdrawal options at NPS maturity at age 60?
ground_truth: At 60, up to 60% of corpus can be withdrawn lump sum tax-free, and at least 40% must be used to buy annuity from empanelled providers. If corpus is under Rs 5 lakh, 100% lump sum is allowed. Commuted annuity income is taxed as pension at slab rate. Delayed withdrawal up to age 75 is permitted with continued contributions.

question: How are NPS returns taxed at exit after the PFRDA 2024 clarification on 60% lump sum?
ground_truth: The 60% lump sum withdrawal at 60 is entirely tax-exempt per 2024 clarification. Only 40% annuity purchase is deferred; annuity payouts are taxed as income when received. Partial withdrawals up to 25% after 3 years for specified reasons remain tax-free.

question: What is the auto-choice versus active choice allocation in NPS and default equity caps?
ground_truth: Active choice lets subscriber set equity (E), corporate bond (C), government securities (G) percentages, with equity capped at 75% until age 50 then tapered. Auto-choice offers three life-cycle funds: Aggressive (LC75), Moderate (LC50), Conservative (LC25) where equity auto-reduces with age. Switch between options allowed twice per year.

question: Can an NRI subscribe to NPS and what are the repatriation restrictions on maturity proceeds?
ground_truth: NRIs aged 18-70 can open NPS (except OCI and persons from FATF-blacklisted nations). Contributions are non-repatriable beyond original repatriable limit; maturity proceeds are credited to NRO account and repatriation limited to USD 1 million per FY under FEMA with CA certificate and tax clearance. Aadhaar-based eKYC is mandatory.

question: What are the partial withdrawal rules for NPS Tier I before retirement?
ground_truth: Up to 25% of employee's own contribution (excluding employer) can be withdrawn after 3 years of account opening for child's education/marriage, house construction, or medical emergency, up to three times with 5-year gap between withdrawals. Withdrawn amount is tax-free and reduces final corpus.

question: How does the employer contribution under Section 80CCD(2) affect take-home salary structuring?
ground_truth: Employer contribution up to 10% of basic+DA (14% for central government) to NPS is deductible under 80CCD(2) without Rs 1.5 lakh ceiling, directly reducing taxable salary. Employee can negotiate higher basic or specific NPS component to utilize this; employer bears no extra cost beyond agreed CTC but must register as corporate NPS model.

question: Is a will mandatory for mutual fund nomination to be legally binding?
ground_truth: Nomination alone makes nominee a trustee for legal heirs, not absolute owner if challenged by will or succession law per Supreme Court 2023 clarification. Will overrides nomination if it specifically bequeaths the folio with clear intent. Without will, nomination facilitates quick transmission but legal heirs can claim via succession certificate.

question: What is the difference between a nominee and a legal heir for insurance proceeds?
ground_truth: Nominee is custodian who receives payout to distribute to legal heirs per succession act unless also a class I heir. Legal heir has ownership per personal law. Since 2015 amendment, policyholder can appoint beneficiary nominee (spouse/children/parents) who then becomes outright owner, shielded from creditors.

question: How should HUF assets be partitioned for succession planning after the 2005 Hindu Succession Amendment?
ground_truth: Post-2005, daughters are coparceners by birth with equal rights in HUF property. Partition requires deed with all coparceners' consent, equal share distribution, and registration for immovable property. HUF dissolution triggers deemed partition for tax; PAN must be surrendered. Will cannot bequeath undivided HUF interest beyond testator's notional share.

question: What are the requirements for a valid will under Indian Succession Act, 1925?
ground_truth: A valid will must be in writing, signed by testator in presence of two attesting witnesses who also sign. Registration is optional but recommended for immovables. Testator must be sound-minded and major. Codicil can amend will with same attestations. Probate is mandatory in Mumbai/Kolkata/Chennai for immovables, optional elsewhere.

question: Explain the role of a trust versus will for managing minor children's financial assets.
ground_truth: A private trust allows trustee management of assets for minors with staggered vesting and protection from early dissipation; will simply bequeaths but requires guardianship until majority at 18. Trust needs deed and registration, can avoid probate, and provides creditor protection. Costs include trustee fees and annual compliance; will is simpler and cheaper initially.
